transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-07
Start time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Jordan Price (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (Apexion - NetEng), Lucas Ortega (Apexion - SecArch), Priya Nair (Apexion - VP Eng)

Auto-summary (auto):
Apexion is evaluating Redwood for private deployments behind their VPC. Primary blockers: static egress IP requirements for downstream vendors, multi-region/data residency (EU + US), and HSM/KMS integration for customer-managed keys. They prefer a Transit-GW style onramp but are open to PrivateLink/Interface endpoints in some regions. Next steps agreed: share connectivity checklist, SOC2/security bundle, and schedule a 2-hour design workshop.

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: Alright everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Jordan from Redwood, AE on this account. We also have Samir, our SE, hi Samir.
[00:08] Samir: Hey all, good to meet you.
[00:10] Priya: Hi, thanks for fitting us in. We're trying to, uh, move quickly on this — we've got a vendor window in Q1.
[00:16] Maya: Yeah, hi, Maya here. I'm the network owner. I'll talk through our VPC stuff.
[00:20] Lucas: Lucas, security architect, I'll focus on compliance and egress constraints.
[00:24] Jordan: Great. High level: Apexion is evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private. Today's focus is private/onramp networking and egress. Samir, do you want to kick off with how Redwood Private typically integrates?
[00:34] Samir: Sure. So Redwood Private exposes a control plane we can either host in our managed control plane or run a private control plane in your VPC — most customers want a VPC onramp using either Transit Gateway or direct peering and interface endpoints (PrivateLink). We support interface VPC endpoints in supported regions, plus static egress via NAT or our egress proxies if you need fixed IPs. Note: some regions have limitations on interface endpoints and cross-account peering.
[01:05] Maya: When you say "fixed IPs" what are the options? We have downstream vendors that only allow whitelisting by IP.
[01:11] Samir: Right. There are two common patterns: 1) You route egress through your NAT Gateway(s) so all outbound traffic to the internet originates from your IP space. That's simple if the model execution sits in your VPC (private deployment). 2) For hosted or dedicated, we can provide a set of static egress IPs via an outbound proxy/NAT managed by Redwood and announce them — but that adds contractual controls.
[01:33] Lucas: So for private, we're basically running compute in our subnets? We want to keep the weights of model data internal — no tokens leaving the region.
[01:40] Samir: Yes, with Redwood Private the inference can run in your subnets. There's an on-prem package or VPC appliance pattern. For cloud VPC deployments we push containers into your accounts and they run using your KMS.
[01:52] Priya: KMS — we use a customer-managed KMS with HSM-backed keys for all encryption at rest. How does Redwood integrate?
[01:58] Samir: We support CMKs on AWS via ARN integration. For HSM you'd use your CloudHSM or an HSM-backed KMS; we can integrate using our connector so we never hold the plaintext keys. We'll send the KMS integration notes in the security pack.
[02:12] Jordan: Quick qual: what regions must you serve from?
[02:16] Priya: Two main loci: eu-west-1 for EU customers and us-east-1 for US ones. We also have a smaller APAC presence in ap-southeast-1 but that's lower priority.
[02:26] Maya: For eu-west-1 we need data residency — inference must not leave eu-west-1 for EU tenant data.
[02:31] Samir: We can pin model versions to region and ensure the serving pool stays in eu-west-1. If you need guaranteed residency we recommend dedicated pools per region, or a VPC-only private deployment with no cross-region traffic.
[02:46] Lucas: A follow-up: audit logs — we need cloudtrail-style logs for all inference requests and administrative actions. Retention 1 year. Can Redwood expose that?
[02:55] Samir: Yes, we can forward audit logs to your logging account — CloudWatch/S3 or a syslog endpoint. We'll include the exact log schema in the security pack. There's an option to redact inputs in logs for PII.
[03:07] Jordan: Maya, can you run us through your current network topology so we can map options?
[03:12] Maya: Sure. We have two AWS accounts for prod (us-east-1 and eu-west-1), both connected via Transit Gateway. CIDR ranges: 10.0.0.0/16 (US), 10.1.0.0/16 (EU). We peer with on-prem via Direct Connect -> Transit GW. Outbound to vendors goes through a pair of NAT gateways in each AZ; we also have an egress firewall appliance that does DLP.
[03:36] Samir: Helpful. So pattern A: Redwood Private deploys into your prod account, uses ENIs and an interface endpoint for control plane traffic, and egress goes through your NATs so vendor traffic originates from your public IPs. Pattern B: If you want Redwood-managed egress IPs we can provide that but it's more typical for hosted customers.
[03:53] Lucas: We're leaning to pattern A. However the egress firewall performs TLS interception; will service-to-service mTLS break that?
[04:00] Samir: If you terminate TLS within the egress device, you'll need to provide the certs or let the egress device perform forward proxying. For mTLS between Redwood pods and services, we can operate in simple TLS or accept mutual TLS if you can provide cert rotation. It's a bit of config work.
[04:17] Priya: For cert rotation — we have an internal Vault workflow. Can Redwood integrate with HashiCorp Vault for cert injection or do you rely only on AWS SSM/Secrets Manager?
[04:27] Samir: We can integrate with Vault via a connector. We'll capture the exact requirements in the security integration doc.
[04:33] Maya: Another constraint — we have strict egress IP mapping by vendor. We need to know if the outbound ports are limited — e.g., some vendor APIs only allow 443 and 5222.
[04:42] Samir: Redwood's model serving makes outbound calls for telemetry, model downloads (initial), and optionally for tool calls/LLM tool integrations. We can control outbound destinations via egress rules; by default we need to reach Redwood's control plane endpoints, model artifact S3 buckets (if using our model catalog) and optionally external tools. We can route artifact retrieval through your S3 if you mirror artifacts.
[05:02] Jordan: This is a good time to talk about artifact hosting — do you plan to use Redwood's catalog models or bring-your-own?
[05:09] Priya: We'll be mostly BYOM — we have finetuned checkpoints and are comfortable storing artifacts in our S3.
[05:14] Samir: Perfect. We support pulling from your S3 via role-assume and signed URLs so artifacts don't need to traverse the public internet.
[05:22] Maya: About peering — we currently use Transit GW for on-prem. If Redwood wants to run in our account, do we need an explicit peering or will the Redwood agents be deployed as cross-account ASG?
[05:33] Samir: We typically provision resources in your account with cross-account IAM so it's not classic VPC Peering. For Transit Gateway attachments, we can attach via a TGW VPC attachment in your account. For PrivateLink, we can create interface endpoints which your team accepts. The exact pattern depends on whether you want isolated subnets and how much control you want.
[05:52] Lucas: Regarding TGW, we have route table segregation and centralized egress — we need to avoid route table conflicts. Will Redwood respect specific route table tags and VPC prefix lists?
[06:01] Samir: Yes. We will follow your tagging and can be excluded from certain route tables; we'll request the exact route table IDs and prefix lists during onboarding.
[06:09] Maya: Ok. Latency expectations: for user-facing completions we need p99 < 250ms token latency in us-east-1 for short prompts. What's feasible?
[06:20] Samir: For small models it's doable; for large chatty models p99 will be higher. If latency is critical, we recommend a dedicated pool pinned in region with autoscale tuned for tail latency, and smaller quantized models to reduce compute. We'll run benchmarks during the SE workshop.
[06:36] Priya: Is there any requirement for inbound NAT or special DNS? We use Private DNS for internal services and split-horizon.
[06:43] Samir: For interface endpoints we can use private DNS. For control-plane we usually register a private hosted zone so services resolve to your VPC-local endpoints. We'll document DNS steps.
[06:53] Jordan: I want to capture any hard blockers — Lucas, from security perspective, is there anything that would stop this?
[06:59] Lucas: Short answer: keys and audit. We need KMS integration for CMKs AND proof that logs can't be modified. Also we require SOC2 Type II and a contractual BAA — we have PHI in some workflows. Do you have a BAA?
[07:12] Jordan: We do offer BAA for enterprise customers — we'll include the legal contact. SOC2 reports will be in the security pack.
[07:19] Samir: For log immutability we can forward to your S3 bucket with object lock or to a central logging account with retention policy.
[07:25] Maya: One more network nuance — we use AWS Network Firewall and expect allowed traffic flows from the Redwood subnets only on egress ports 443/80, plus a small set of vendor-specific ports.
[07:36] Samir: We can provide a list of Redwood outbound FQDNs and IP ranges for your firewall allowlist. For private deployments those FQDNs will resolve to internal ENIs so traffic stays in your VPC.
[07:48] Priya: About failover — if an AZ fails, we need no more than 5-10s to failover for critical endpoints. Is that in scope?
[07:56] Samir: We recommend multi-AZ deployment for control and serving; failover times vary but multi-AZ with health checks can be sub-second for some flows. For long-running completion sessions, KV cache warmup can add latency; we suggest active-active across AZs for best behavior.
[08:12] Jordan: Let's talk cost/packaging briefly — are you leaning to Dedicated reserved capacity or Private?
[08:18] Priya: We'd prefer Private if we can meet security and egress requirements. Dedicated is attractive for predictable pricing but doesn't solve our data residency waits.
[08:27] Jordan: Ok. We'll prepare cost delta for dedicated vs private with estimated token/sec workloads.
[08:33] Maya: Also, we have a strict IP allowlist process for vendors — change windows are every month. We need a plan for adding Redwood IPs into that schedule.
[08:43] Samir: Understood. We'll provide a minimal initial allowlist and a change workflow doc. We can also use an SSM parameter or a secrets store for dynamic IP updates if your firewall supports that.
[08:56] Lucas: I want to workshop the TGW attachment model — can you show us a diagram or propose a config?
[09:02] Samir: Yes — that's part of the SE workshop. Proposed agenda: 1) Review current VPC CIDRs and TGW route tables; 2) Decide between interface endpoint vs TGW attachment per region; 3) KMS / key access, audit log routing; 4) Egress IP and firewall allowlist; 5) Pilot plan and rollback.
[09:21] Priya: Two-hour session sounds right. Next Tuesday would work for us.
[09:25] Jordan: We'll send a meeting poll; Samir will prep the diagrams.
[09:29] Maya: Can you confirm which regions Redwood supports interface endpoints in? We had issues with some vendors in ap-southeast.
[09:36] Samir: We'll include a region matrix in the checklist. Generally most major clouds have endpoints in common regions, but some internal infra like our artifact registry may be hosted only in us-east-1. We'll provide multi-region artifact mirroring options.
[09:52] Jordan: Quick note on shared artifacts — Samir mentioned you can pull artifacts from your S3. That avoids public download.
[09:58] Samir: Yes, we can assume an IAM role or use signed URLs.
[10:02] Lucas: Compliance question: if Redwood runs control plane outside our accounts, do we get visibility into control-plane logs?
[10:08] Samir: You can get control plane telemetry forwarded; for full separation we can offer a private control plane deployed in your account. That meets higher compliance thresholds.
[10:18] Priya: Ok. Anything else on network?
[10:21] Maya: One smaller ask: our egress device rewrites SNI. Will that break any of your cert expectations?
[10:27] Samir: It might for mTLS. We'll need to test in the SE workshop.
[10:31] Jordan: I'm going to open the parking lot — any non-network blockers?
[10:34] Priya: From engineering: performance tests, can you run a synthetic workload with our prompt set in us-east-1 to validate p99?
[10:42] Samir: Yes. We'll ask for the prompt set and sample traffic profile. We'll include benchmark steps in the workshop.
[10:48] Maya: Also, who will own the infra costs for storage of artifacts mirrored into our S3? We assume Apexion pays storage; Redwood pays compute if running in Redwood-managed infra?
[10:58] Jordan: Correct. If compute runs in your account (private), you'd pay the cloud compute and we bill for Redwood software license; if we run dedicated in our infra, Redwood bears compute cost as part of dedicated pricing. We'll lay out the split in the cost doc.
[11:12] Lucas: Last question: are there any known gotchas for Direct Connect + TGW when attaching a vendor-managed VPC? We want to avoid asymmetrical routing.
[11:20] Samir: Avoid overlapping CIDRs and ensure TGW route propagation is controlled. We'll provide recommended route table layouts. For asymmetry, prefer VGW+TGW attachments or explicit route propagation controls.
[11:30] Jordan: Alright let's recap and confirm next steps.
[11:33] Jordan: Action items: we'll send the connectivity checklist, SOC2 and KMS notes, and schedule the SE workshop. Samir: you'll prep the TGW/PE diagram and benchmark plan. Maya: please share CIDRs and peering configs. Lucas: we'll coordinate on BAA/legal.
[11:50] Priya: Sounds good. One more — can you share a sample network diagram now?
[11:54] Samir: I'll drop an initial sketch in the follow-up email; it's basic but shows TGW attachment and interface endpoints.
[11:59] Jordan: Great. We'll target the workshop for next Tuesday. Thanks everyone.
[12:04] Maya: Thanks.
[12:06] Lucas: Thanks all.
[52:00] End of call.
